explanation: You nailed it! Conization takes out a cone-shaped wedge of the cervix containing the abnormal cells. Because the rest of the uterus is left alone, future pregnancies are still possible. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T10#GNS313_U3_T10_h7)

question: Why do doctors frequently combine chemotherapy with radiation therapy when treating advanced cervical cancer?

options.A: Chemotherapy prevents all future infections in the urinary tract
options.B: Chemotherapy drugs make cancer cells more sensitive to radiation damage
options.C: Radiation destroys the chemotherapy drugs before they harm healthy tissue
options.D: Chemotherapy eliminates the need for surgical removal of lymph nodes

explanation: Great clinical insight! In this case, the chemotherapy drugs act as helpers (radiosensitizers) that make the cancer cells weaker and much more vulnerable to being destroyed by the radiation. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T10#GNS313_U3_T10_h7)

question: As a nurse, what major emotional or psychological challenge should you anticipate for a patient facing a radical hysterectomy?

options.A: Complete loss of long-term memory function
options.B: Sudden denial of the physical diagnosis by family members
options.C: Intense fear of hospital food and environmental sounds
options.D: Body image disturbance and grief over lost fertility

explanation: Spot on. Losing reproductive organs can trigger profound emotional grief regarding womanhood, body image, and the ability to have children. Compassionate nursing support is everything here. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T10#GNS313_U3_T10_h8)

question: A patient with advanced terminal cervical cancer is in severe, constant pain in her pelvis and back. What is your top nursing priority?

options.A: Preparing the patient for emergency radical pelvic surgery
options.B: Encouraging the patient to walk outside to distract her from the pain
options.C: Administering prescribed analgesics regularly based on pain assessment
options.D: Restricting fluid intake to decrease pressure on the pelvic organs

explanation: You've got it. In palliative care, keeping the patient comfortable through regular, structured pain relief is a top priority to preserve their dignity and quality of life. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T10#GNS313_U3_T10_h8)

question: At what age group are public health programs primarily targeting the HPV vaccine for the best results?

options.A: Pre-adolescent girls aged 9 to 14 years
options.B: Infants during their routine immunization schedule
options.C: Adult women over the age of 50 years
options.D: Pregnant women during prenatal clinic visits

explanation: Correct! The HPV vaccine works best when given before any exposure to the virus through sexual activity, which is why pre-teens aged 9 to 14 are the main target group. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T10#GNS313_U3_T10_h9)

question: Even if a woman has received the HPV vaccine, why must she still go for regular cervical cancer screening later in life?

options.A: The vaccines do not protect against all high-risk strains of HPV
options.B: Screening tests are required to check if the vaccine was absorbed
options.C: Vaccinated individuals have a higher risk of developing infections
options.D: The vaccine wears off completely after exactly five years

explanation: Spot on! While the vaccine defends against the most common cancer-causing HPV strains, other less common high-risk strains can still cause issues, making regular screening still necessary. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T10#GNS313_U3_T10_h9)

question: Which type of lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed in clinical practice?

options.A: Bronchial Carcinoid Tumor
options.B: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
options.C: Small Cell Lung Cancer
options.D: Primary Pleural Mesothelioma

explanation: You've got this! Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer accounts for about 85% of all lung cancer cases, making it much more common than the small cell type. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h1)

question: Why is Small Cell Lung Cancer usually treated with medications (systemic therapy) rather than surgery right away?

options.A: It only occurs in patients who are too old for operations.
options.B: It grows extremely slowly inside the main bronchial tubes.
options.C: It usually spreads to other body parts very early before detection.
options.D: It is completely resistant to any form of surgical removal.

explanation: Great thinking! Small cell lung cancer grows fast and tends to spread (metastasize) early, meaning surgery alone usually isn't enough to catch it all. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h1)

question: After cigarette smoking, what is recognized as the second leading cause of lung cancer?

options.A: Radon gas exposure
options.B: Asbestos inhalation
options.C: Secondhand tobacco smoke
options.D: Airborne coal dust

explanation: Spot on! Radon is a natural radioactive gas that can build up in buildings. After smoking, it's the next big culprit behind lung cancer. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h2)

question: A patient who has never smoked in their life develops lung cancer. Which workplace exposure is a very likely culprit?

options.A: Excessive carbon dioxide
options.B: Household bleach
options.C: Asbestos fibers
options.D: Pure oxygen gas

explanation: Well done! Breathing in asbestos dust on the job is a well-known risk factor that can cause severe lung damage and cancer, even in non-smokers. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h2)

question: What is usually the first sign that makes a patient say, 'I need to get this cough checked out'?

options.A: A persistent, worsening cough
options.B: Sudden complete blindness
options.C: Inability to swallow food
options.D: Severe lower abdominal pain

explanation: Exactly! A new cough that just won't go away is the most common early warning sign of a lung issue. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h3)

question: Why do many lung cancer patients only discover they are sick when the disease is already advanced?

options.A: The lungs lack pain receptors, allowing tumors to grow undetected initially.
options.B: Symptoms only appear after the cancer completely destroys the heart.
options.C: Early lung tumors cause immediate total paralysis of the limbs.
options.D: Blood tests detect the cancer cells only during late stages.

explanation: You got it! Because lung tissue doesn't have pain nerve endings, a small tumor can grow quietly for a long time without causing any physical pain. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h3)

question: Which test gives doctors the final, definitive confirmation that a patient has lung cancer?

options.A: Pulmonary function test
options.B: Tissue biopsy
options.C: Routine chest X-ray
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: Spot on! Scans can strongly suggest cancer, but a pathologist needs to look at an actual tissue sample under a microscope to confirm it. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the main goal of using the TNM staging system for lung cancer?

options.A: To determine the extent of disease spread and plan appropriate treatment
options.B: To measure the exact volume of air the lungs can hold
options.C: To calculate the patient's exact daily calorie requirements
options.D: To identify which specific type of cigarette the patient smoked

explanation: Brilliant! TNM helps the team figure out how big the tumor is, if it has reached lymph nodes, and how far it has spread, guiding the best treatment plan. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the main goal when a patient is caught early with non-small cell lung cancer?

options.A: Total lung transplantation
options.B: Surgical resection
options.C: Palliative hospice care
options.D: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy

explanation: You're doing great! If the cancer is caught early and hasn't spread, cutting out the tumor surgically gives the best chance for a complete cure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h5)

question: How does immunotherapy work differently from standard chemotherapy?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for any diagnostic imaging procedures.
options.B: It only acts on the outer layer of the skin and never reaches the lungs.
options.C: It freezes the tumor tissue by lowering the core body temperature.
options.D: It empowers the body's own immune defenses to target and destroy cancer cells.

explanation: Exactly right! Instead of just attacking cells directly like chemo, immunotherapy helps your own white blood cells recognize and fight off the cancer. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h5)

question: As a nurse, what is the quickest way to help a patient who is suddenly struggling to catch their breath due to lung cancer?

options.A: Laying the patient flat on their back in bed
options.B: Placing the patient in a high-Fowler's position
options.C: Encouraging rapid, shallow mouth breathing
options.D: Restricting all fluid intake for twelve hours

explanation: Spot on, nurse! Sitting the patient upright in a high-Fowler's position lets their chest expand fully, making it much easier to draw breath. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h6)

question: A patient who just had lung surgery is scared to cough because their incision hurts. What should you, the nurse, do first?

options.A: Tell the patient that coughing is optional and let them sleep all day.
options.B: Apply a tight chest binder to completely immobilize the chest wall.
options.C: Administer prescribed pain medication before encouraging controlled coughing exercises.
options.D: Report the patient immediately to the surgeon for emergency re-operation.

explanation: Wonderful clinical judgment! Controlling the pain first allows the patient to cough and clear their lungs safely without agony, preventing complications like collapsed lung areas. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h6)

question: Which screening tool is best for catching lung cancer early in high-risk people who don't have symptoms yet?

options.A: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.B: Standard routine sputum culture
options.C: Pulmonary spirometry test
options.D: Low-dose computed tomography scan

explanation: You've got this! A low-dose CT scan captures clear images of the lungs using very low radiation, making it the gold standard for high-risk screening. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h7)

question: Why is quitting smoking considered 'primary prevention' rather than 'secondary prevention'?

options.A: It is only performed after a patient receives a confirmed cancer diagnosis.
options.B: It relies entirely on surgical removal of damaged bronchial tissue.
options.C: It focuses on finding small tumors before symptoms appear.
options.D: It aims to prevent the disease from ever developing in the first place.

explanation: Brilliant! Primary prevention stops harmful exposures (like tobacco) so the disease process never even gets a chance to start. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h7)

question: What best defines an accident in community health terms?

options.A: A planned medical procedure with complications
options.B: A chronic disease with a slow onset
options.C: An unexpected event causing injury or harm
options.D: An unavoidable natural health disaster

explanation: Accidents are sudden, unexpected events that cause physical harm or damage to individuals. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h1)

question: Why do community health nurses look at accidents as things we can prevent rather than just 'bad luck'?

options.A: Because bad luck cannot be studied scientifically
options.B: Because most accidents follow preventable patterns
options.C: Because hospitals profit directly from treating injuries
options.D: Because government policies cause all accidents

explanation: Spotting accidents as preventable events helps us design safety steps that keep our communities safe and injury-free! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h1)

question: Which type of accident causes the highest number of injuries and trauma on Nigerian roads?

options.A: Road traffic accidents
options.B: Commercial flight crashes
options.C: Skiing and snowboarding falls
options.D: Mountain climbing injuries

explanation: Crashes involving cars, commercial buses, motorcycles, and pedestrians are among the leading causes of trauma in our country. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h2)

question: A toddler in a home suffers skin burns from a pot of hot soup on the floor. What kind of accident is this?

options.A: An occupational accident
options.B: A domestic accident
options.C: A road traffic accident
options.D: An industrial accident

explanation: Mishaps like burns, cuts, and falls that happen right inside or around the home environment are called domestic accidents. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h2)

question: Storing kerosene inside an empty soft drink bottle is an example of which type of risk factor at home?

options.A: Chronic medical illness
options.B: Hereditary predisposition
options.C: Environmental hazard
options.D: Psychological disorder

explanation: Putting dangerous liquids in drink bottles creates an unsafe home environment that easily leads to accidental poisoning or burns. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h3)

question: What is the main reason young children experience so many domestic accidents?

options.A: Lack of proper formal education in school
options.B: A deliberate desire to break household rules
options.C: An inherited weakness in motor coordination
options.D: Natural curiosity combined with unsafe surroundings

explanation: Children love to explore their world! When dangerous items are left within their reach, accidents can easily happen. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h3)

question: What is a very common emotional challenge faced by people who survive severe road crashes?

options.A: Complete emotional numbness to joy
options.B: Increased physical stamina
options.C: Post-traumatic stress disorder
options.D: Enhanced memory retention

explanation: Survivors of violent crashes often deal with lingering emotional trauma, anxiety, and flashbacks, known as PTSD. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h4)

question: How do major community accidents immediately affect local hospitals and clinics?

options.A: By eliminating the need for surgical supplies
options.B: By overwhelming emergency wards and depleting blood banks
options.C: By reducing the overall cost of running the hospital
options.D: By increasing the number of available nurses on duty

explanation: A sudden rush of trauma patients can quickly stretch hospital supplies, staff, and blood reserves to their limits. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h4)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the emergency ABCDE assessment framework?

options.A: Breathing
options.B: Blood pressure
options.C: Bleeding
options.D: Bone fracture

explanation: In emergency triage, B stands for breathing to ensure the victim is receiving adequate oxygen exchange. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h5)

question: A patient is rescued from a motorcycle crash with suspected spinal cord damage. What is the safest immediate action?

options.A: Encourage the patient to stand up and walk quickly
options.B: Twist the neck sideways to check for flexibility
options.C: Drag the victim rapidly by the arms to the clinic
options.D: Avoid unnecessary movement to protect the spine

explanation: Carelessly moving someone with a potential spinal injury can cause permanent paralysis. Always keep them still and protect the spine! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h5)

question: Why is getting accident victims out of bed and moving early so important during recovery?

options.A: To increase hospital discharge fees
options.B: To make nursing documentation harder
options.C: To eliminate the need for physical therapy
options.D: To prevent pressure sores and blood clots

explanation: Early mobilization helps prevent nasty complications of being stuck in bed, like pressure ulcers and deep vein thrombosis. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h6)

question: Which healthcare professional helps recovering accident victims relearn everyday tasks like dressing, bathing, and eating?

options.A: Occupational therapist
options.B: Hospital pharmacist
options.C: Laboratory technician
options.D: Radiology specialist

explanation: Occupational therapists are fantastic at helping patients regain practical skills for daily living and independence. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h6)

question: What is the main goal of community-based accident prevention programs?

options.A: Building larger trauma wards in every city
options.B: Stopping accidents before they happen through education
options.C: Increasing the supply of emergency surgical gloves
options.D: Training more mortuary attendants

explanation: Prevention is all about spotting risks early and educating the public so accidents never happen in the first place. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h7)

question: A community health nurse wants to reduce head injuries among local commercial motorcycle riders. What is the best step to take?

options.A: Fines for patients who report to the hospital injured
options.B: Closing down all commercial transport businesses
options.C: Conducting safety campaigns on proper helmet use with riders
options.D: Waiting in the clinic to treat victims as they arrive

explanation: Working directly with transport riders to promote safety education and helmet use is a proven way to prevent severe head trauma. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h7)

question: In basic terms, what is a poison?

options.A: Any substance that disrupts body functions or causes harm when introduced
options.B: A prescription drug taken strictly according to doctor instructions
options.C: A chemical compound that only harms the liver and kidneys
options.D: An infectious microorganism found in contaminated water sources

explanation: Spot on! A poison is simply anything that enters the body and causes harm or upsets normal body functions. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h1)

question: Why are toddlers so prone to accidental poisoning at home?

options.A: Their natural curiosity drives them to taste and explore colorful items
options.B: Parents frequently leave dangerous medications inside school bags
options.C: Toddlers are usually employed to handle agricultural pesticides
options.D: They possess a high genetic tolerance for household chemicals

explanation: Exactly! Little ones love to explore everything using their mouths, often mistaking bright chemicals or syrups for sweet treats. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h1)

question: In Nigerian homes, which household liquid is most often accidentally swallowed by children because it's stored in empty drink bottles?

options.A: Clean water
options.B: Cooking oil
options.C: Fruit juice
options.D: Kerosene

explanation: Well done! Storing kerosene in old soft drink bottles is a major hazard because kids easily mistake it for water or juice. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h2)

question: What makes farming pesticides particularly dangerous in rural areas?

options.A: Farmers use them exclusively as food flavoring agents in local dishes
options.B: They are frequently stored near food items and handled without protective gear
options.C: They only affect animals and have zero toxic impact on human physiology
options.D: They lose their toxicity completely within a few minutes of application

explanation: Spot on! When chemicals are kept close to food and used without gloves or masks, accidental poisoning happens easily. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h2)

question: Through which route do gases or vapors enter the bloodstream the fastest?

options.A: Inhalation
options.B: Subcutaneous contact
options.C: Ingestion
options.D: Skin absorption

explanation: You got it! Breathing in a gas sends it straight through the huge surface area of the lungs directly into the blood. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h3)

question: How do organophosphate poisons mess with the nervous system?

options.A: By blocking acetylcholinesterase and causing neurotransmitter accumulation
options.B: By drying up all bodily fluids through immediate kidney failure
options.C: By turning the blood acidic within seconds of skin contact
options.D: By freezing the spinal cord to completely stop all nerve impulses

explanation: That's right! They block the enzyme that normally cleans up acetylcholine, meaning nerves keep firing continuously without a break. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h3)

question: Which sign is a classic giveaway of an opioid overdose?

options.A: Pinpoint pupils
options.B: Extreme pupil dilation
options.C: Uncontrollable muscle tremors
options.D: Severe skin redness and sweating

explanation: Spot on! Tiny, pinpoint pupils combined with slow breathing are classic red flags for opioid overdose. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h4)

question: A farmer arrives at the clinic drooling, tearing up, peeing frequently, and having muscle twitches after spraying the farm. What is this?

options.A: Sedative overdose from sleeping pills
options.B: Cholinergic poisoning from organophosphates
options.C: Caustic poisoning from swallowed acid
options.D: Opioid poisoning from strong painkillers

explanation: Correct! Remember the DUMBELS sign (drooling, urination, muscle twitching, etc.)—it points straight to organophosphate poisoning. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h4)

question: Why should you NEVER make a patient vomit after they swallow kerosene?

options.A: It makes the poison taste much worse on its way back up
options.B: It can cause the chemical to enter the lungs and cause aspiration pneumonia
options.C: It immediately neutralizes all medications given in the hospital
options.D: It causes instant blindness in both eyes

explanation: Well done! Coming back up, kerosene can easily slip into the windpipe and lungs, causing severe chemical pneumonia. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h5)

question: What is the immediate nursing action if a chemical splashes into a patient's eyes?

options.A: Wait for laboratory blood test results before touching the face
options.B: Cover the eyes tightly with dry gauze bandages without washing
options.C: Flush the eyes continuously with clean water for at least fifteen minutes
options.D: Apply concentrated acid neutralizer drops directly to the corneas

explanation: Spot on! Quick and long flushing with clean water washes the chemical away before it can permanently damage the cornea. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h5)

question: What is the best way to prevent accidental poisoning in community health?

options.A: Building specialized intensive care units in every village clinic
options.B: Educating families on proper chemical storage and prohibiting food-container reuse
options.C: Training traditional healers to perform emergency gastric lavage
options.D: Banning the sale of all cleaning agents and agricultural chemicals

explanation: Correct! Teaching families how to safely store items and never use old drink bottles for chemicals stops poisonings before they happen. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h6)

question: Which of these is a WRONG practice when it comes to preventing poisoning?

options.A: Using clear labeling on all containers holding hazardous substances
options.B: Storing kerosene and bleach in empty soft drink bottles in the kitchen
options.C: Consulting qualified health workers before taking herbal concoctions
options.D: Keeping all pharmaceutical drugs locked up away from children

explanation: You got it! Putting dangerous chemicals in drink bottles is a recipe for disaster. Always keep them in their original, clearly labeled containers. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h6)

question: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) define violence?

options.A: Severe property damage resulting from civil unrest or political conflict
options.B: The unlawful imprisonment of an individual without formal legal charges
options.C: Any accidental injury sustained during a physical altercation in a public space
options.D: The intentional use of physical force or power against oneself, another person, or a group

explanation: Spot on! The key word here is *intentional*. The WHO looks at force or power used on purpose that either causes or risks harm. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h1)

question: As a nurse, why is it important to look beyond obvious physical injuries when checking for abuse?

options.A: Because abusers always come along to every hospital visit
options.B: Because physical injuries always heal completely without leaving emotional scars
options.C: Because hospital rules do not allow us to write down emotional abuse
options.D: Because victims often come in with vague aches and pains instead of visible cuts or bruises

explanation: You've got this! Abuse shows up in many hidden ways. Patients might visit the clinic complaining of ongoing headaches, tiredness, or belly pain rather than obvious trauma. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h1)

question: What is the main feature of self-directed violence?

options.A: It involves organized groups fighting for political power
options.B: The victim and the perpetrator are the same person
options.C: It is always done by close family members
options.D: It happens only in crowded city areas

explanation: Exactly! Self-directed violence means actions someone inflicts on themselves, such as self-harm or suicide attempts. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h2)

question: If two strangers get into a physical fight at a busy local market, what type of violence is this considered?

options.A: Intimate partner violence
options.B: Community violence
options.C: Collective violence
options.D: Self-directed violence

explanation: Well done! When violence happens outside the home between people who are unrelated and often don't know each other, we call it community violence. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h2)

question: Which of the following is a well-known risk factor for future violent behavior?

options.A: Consistently achieving a high level of formal education
options.B: Living in a household with little to no financial debt
options.C: Taking an active part in school or community sports
options.D: Experiencing abuse or trauma during childhood

explanation: Spot on! Early childhood trauma and seeing domestic abuse at home are strong warning signs for experiencing or committing violence later in life. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h3)

question: How should nurses view community challenges like poverty and lack of education when looking at health risks?

options.A: As permanent problems that public health programs can never fix
options.B: As important warning signs to help us protect vulnerable people
options.C: As proof that a specific person will definitely commit a crime
options.D: As minor issues that have no real effect on mental health

explanation: Great thinking! Understanding these root causes helps nurses and public health teams focus their support where it's needed most. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h3)

question: Which mental health issue is most commonly diagnosed in survivors of severe violence?

options.A: Bipolar mood disorder
options.B: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
options.C: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
options.D: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)

explanation: Correct! Survivors of intense physical, emotional, or sexual trauma very often develop PTSD because of the deep impact of their experience. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h4)

question: A patient comes to the clinic with ongoing pelvic pain and high anxiety, and hints point toward past abuse. What does this show us?

options.A: That physical injuries from violence always heal completely in a few weeks
options.B: That mental health struggles never cause physical pain in the body
options.C: That chronic physical symptoms and emotional trauma are often connected
options.D: That the patient is just making up symptoms to get drugs

explanation: Spot on! Violence often leaves lasting physical pain right alongside deep emotional scars, which is why holistic nursing care is so important. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h4)

question: Which group of people faces a much higher risk of experiencing interpersonal violence?

options.A: Retired corporate executives
options.B: Middle-aged professional athletes
options.C: Pregnant women and young children
options.D: Healthy young adult males living by themselves

explanation: You got it! Vulnerable groups like pregnant women, children, and older adults statistically experience higher rates of abuse and neglect. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h5)

question: Why is it so important to create a private, judgment-free space when screening a patient for abuse?

options.A: To stop the patient from asking questions about their drugs
options.B: To follow hospital billing rules for emergency room visits
options.C: To help the patient feel safe enough to share sensitive information
options.D: To make sure the doctor finishes the physical exam quickly

explanation: Exactly! Victims of violence often hide what happened out of fear or shame. Privacy and a warm, safe approach make all the difference. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h5)

question: What is a key part of a safety plan made for someone who has experienced violence?

options.A: Quitting your job right away without any money saved
options.B: Confronting the abuser face-to-face in a public place
options.C: Knowing safe places to go and packing important documents
options.D: Avoiding all contact with healthcare workers and social workers

explanation: Well done! A practical safety plan helps someone leave quickly if danger gets worse, including knowing where to find shelter and keeping vital papers ready. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h6)

question: Why do we need different sectors—like health, law enforcement, and social services—to work together when managing violence cases?

options.A: Because police officers must approve all nursing care plans
options.B: Because survivors need medical, legal, social, and psychological support
options.C: Because hospital nurses have the legal power to arrest criminals
options.D: Because social workers are the only ones allowed to treat physical injuries

explanation: Spot on! No single profession can fix every problem a violence survivor faces. Teamwork across health, law, and social services is essential. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h6)

question: What does a "double burden of disease" mean in Nigerian public health?

options.A: Having high rates of both maternal and child mortality simultaneously
options.B: Suffering from simultaneous outbreaks of waterborne and airborne infections
options.C: Managing high patient loads in both rural clinics and urban teaching hospitals
options.D: Dealing with both infectious diseases and chronic non-communicable diseases

explanation: Great job! A double burden simply means our healthcare system has to fight old enemies like malaria and TB while also managing the rising wave of lifestyle diseases like hypertension and diabetes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why do non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like hypertension often go unnoticed for years?

options.A: Symptoms only appear after a person reaches retirement age
options.B: They develop silently in the body without immediate noticeable symptoms
options.C: Standard diagnostic laboratory tests cannot detect chronic illnesses early
options.D: Patients refuse to visit primary health centres for routine check-ups

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like high blood pressure creep up slowly without causing obvious pain or distress. That's why routine checks are so important for your patients. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h1)

question: How is Behavioural Change Communication (BCC) different from basic health education?

options.A: Basic health education focuses exclusively on preventing infectious diseases
options.B: BCC is only used inside hospital wards by qualified physicians and nurse specialists
options.C: BCC uses interactive dialogue and addresses social obstacles rather than just giving facts
options.D: Basic health education relies heavily on mass media television broadcasts

explanation: You've got it! While basic education just tells people what to do, BCC actually talks *with* them to figure out what's stopping them from living healthier lives. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h2)

question: A nurse wants to address high salt intake in a local market. What should be the very first step?

options.A: Engage market vendors in a discussion about how they view salt use in local foods
options.B: Ban the sale of heavily salted processed snacks within the market stalls
options.C: Organize a mandatory lecture hall seminar for all registered market traders
options.D: Distribute brightly coloured pamphlets detailing the dangers of hypertension

explanation: Brilliant! True nursing care starts with listening. Always involve the community and understand their perspective before trying to change their habits. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h2)

question: According to the Health Belief Model, what must a patient believe first before they will change a health habit?

options.A: The government has implemented strict laws banning unhealthy food imports
options.B: Their local primary healthcare clinic is fully funded and well-equipped
options.C: Their family members have already suffered from the same chronic illness
options.D: They are personally vulnerable to the health condition and see benefits in changing

explanation: Correct! Patients won't change unless they genuinely believe "this can happen to me" and that taking action will actually make a difference for them. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h3)

question: Why is knowing the stages of the Transtheoretical Model useful for a clinical nurse?

options.A: It accurately predicts the exact day a patient will stop smoking or exercising
options.B: It helps tailor counselling to match the patient's exact readiness to change
options.C: It proves whether a patient has a genetic predisposition to chronic illness
options.D: It replaces the need for physical assessments during routine clinic visits

explanation: Exactly right! People change at their own pace. Knowing their stage helps you meet them where they are instead of pushing too hard too fast. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h3)

question: What is the main goal of conducting a community risk factor assessment for NCDs?

options.A: To penalize local food vendors who sell cheap processed carbohydrate meals
options.B: To secure international funding grants for building specialized cardiac hospitals
options.C: To gather local data and identify specific health needs before planning interventions
options.D: To diagnose individual patients with hypertension during routine house calls

explanation: Spot on! You can't solve a problem until you understand it. Assessing the community helps you design programs that actually fit their real-life struggles. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h4)

question: Why should nurses avoid applying urban health assumptions directly to rural farming communities in Nigeria?

options.A: Rural and urban populations often have very different physical activity levels and dietary realities
options.B: Medical diagnostic equipment is completely unavailable outside major state capitals
options.C: Rural communities are completely immune to lifestyle-related chronic health conditions
options.D: Urban residents never participate in focus group discussions or health interviews

explanation: You nailed it! City life and village life are completely different. What works for an office worker in Lagos might make zero sense for a farmer in a rural community. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h4)

question: Which strategy works best when designing health messages for communities with low literacy levels?

options.A: Using pictorial guides, local radio jingles, and interactive drama performances
options.B: Relying entirely on detailed medical charts during community lectures
options.C: Distributing dense academic textbooks written in English about chronic diseases
options.D: Requiring all participants to read online health blogs before clinic visits

explanation: Wonderful! Pictures, local drama, and radio bypass reading barriers, making health education fun and easy for everyone to understand. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h5)

question: A community links weight gain with high social status, making residents resistant to weight-loss advice. What is the best nursing approach?

options.A: Reframing the message around maintaining physical strength and caring for grandchildren
options.B: Stopping health education entirely until local cultural traditions change
options.C: Focusing solely on prescription weight-loss medications available at the pharmacy
options.D: Telling them bluntly that their cultural beliefs are outdated and dangerous

explanation: Smart nursing! Good community nurses respect local culture while gently connecting healthy habits to things the people already care about deeply, like family. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h5)

question: Why is interpersonal communication considered the gold standard for changing health behaviour?

options.A: It reaches thousands of people simultaneously across multiple states
options.B: It allows for direct feedback, personal questions, and tailored guidance
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for community health workers
options.D: It costs significantly less money than printing mass media flyers

explanation: Correct! Nothing beats a real conversation. One-on-one time gives patients the chance to voice their fears and get advice built just for them. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is the biggest advantage of using local community radio stations for NCD health campaigns?

options.A: They replace the need for physical clinical screening examinations
options.B: They can broadcast messages in indigenous languages to reach remote areas
options.C: They are exclusively funded by international public health organizations
options.D: They guarantee that every listener will immediately adopt a healthy diet

explanation: Spot on! Radio bridges the gap, bringing vital health messages right into homes and farms using the local dialects people speak every day. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h6)

question: What common economic challenge often forces families to rely heavily on cheap, refined carbohydrate meals?

options.A: A total lack of agricultural land for farming throughout the entire country
options.B: Financial poverty that makes fresh vegetables and lean proteins expensive
options.C: Universal free distribution of processed foods at primary healthcare centres
options.D: Strict government bans on importing nutritious food items into local markets

explanation: You've got it. Economic reality plays a huge role in health. When fresh protein and veggies are pricey, families naturally turn to cheaper, filling carbs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h7)

question: A patient tells you they are too busy with work and transport to visit the gym. What is your best response as a nurse?

options.A: Tell them that exercise is optional if they take their blood pressure medication
options.B: Advise them to stop working so hard and prioritize leisure time instead
options.C: Suggest simple physical activities that can be built directly into daily chores and routines
options.D: Insist that they must find time for a structured gym membership every evening

explanation: Brilliant! Health advice has to be practical. Recommending things like walking more or active housework fits right into their busy schedules without costing extra money. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h7)

question: What does "process monitoring" evaluate during a community health campaign?

options.A: The exact financial profit generated by local primary health clinics
options.B: Long-term genetic changes in the community's disease risk profile
options.C: The total number of hospital beds required for severe stroke patients
options.D: Day-to-day activities like attendance numbers and media broadcasts

explanation: Correct! Process monitoring is just checking your daily checklist: Are the workshops running? Are people showing up? Did the radio jingle play? [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h8)

question: Why is long-term sustainability such an important goal for community health programs?

options.A: It guarantees that nurses will receive permanent salary increases from the state
options.B: It ensures health promotion continues after external project funding eventually stops
options.C: It prevents infectious disease outbreaks from occurring in urban slums
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for future community health assessments

explanation: Spot on! External grants and projects eventually end. Building local community leadership ensures that the good work keeps going long after outsiders leave. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h8)

question: What do we call the top number in a blood pressure reading?

options.A: Atmospheric pressure
options.B: Systolic pressure
options.C: Diastolic pressure
options.D: Pulse pressure

explanation: Spot on! The top number measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats. That's your systolic pressure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is high blood pressure often called a 'silent killer'?

options.A: It stops the heart completely without warning signs.
options.B: It causes sudden deafness before any physical pain starts.
options.C: It rarely produces early symptoms until serious organ damage occurs.
options.D: It only strikes individuals while they are fast asleep at night.

explanation: You got it! High blood pressure can quietly damage the body for years without any warning signs, which is why regular checks are so important. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h1)

question: What does 'primary hypertension' mean?

options.A: High blood pressure with no single identifiable medical cause
options.B: Blood pressure that only affects young children and infants
options.C: High blood pressure caused by a single known kidney disease
options.D: A temporary spike in pressure caused by severe acute stress

explanation: Exactly! Primary (or essential) hypertension develops gradually over time without one specific underlying medical trigger. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h2)

question: How does eating too much salt contribute to high blood pressure?

options.A: It causes fluid retention which increases total blood volume.
options.B: It directly weakens the heart valves causing backflow.
options.C: It thickens the red blood cells so they cannot move easily.
options.D: It instantly melts the protective lining inside the veins.

explanation: Spot on! Salt (sodium) holds water in your body. This extra fluid increases the total volume of blood pushing against your vessel walls. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h2)

question: A nurse uses a blood pressure cuff that is far too small for an adult patient with a large arm. What kind of reading is most likely to result?

options.A: A falsely low blood pressure reading
options.B: A reading showing zero systolic pressure
options.C: A falsely high blood pressure reading
options.D: A completely normal and accurate reading

explanation: Using a cuff that is too small requires excessive pressure to occlude the branch artery, leading to an artificially inflated blood pressure measurement. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which symptom is a classic warning sign of severely high blood pressure?

options.A: Painful swelling of the ankle joints
options.B: Sudden uncontrollable shivering
options.C: Severe yellowing of the skin
options.D: Early morning occipital headache

explanation: Correct! A throbbing headache at the back of the head, especially right when waking up, is a classic sign of very high blood pressure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h3)

question: What foods does the DASH diet mainly encourage patients to eat?

options.A: Red meats and refined white sugar
options.B: Fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy
options.C: Saturated fats and fried foods
options.D: High-sodium canned and processed meals

explanation: Spot on! The DASH diet focuses on whole foods packed with potassium, calcium, and magnesium to help keep blood pressure in check. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h4)

question: How does regular exercise help manage high blood pressure over time?

options.A: It replaces the need for kidneys to filter excess body water.
options.B: It blocks cholesterol from entering the bloodstream entirely.
options.C: It reduces systemic vascular resistance and strengthens the heart.
options.D: It permanently thickens the walls of the heart chambers.

explanation: Great job! Staying active helps your heart pump more efficiently and lowers the resistance in your blood vessels. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why must you teach patients never to stop their blood pressure medication suddenly?

options.A: It leads to sudden severe hair loss within hours.
options.B: It permanently damages the liver enzymes.
options.C: It can trigger dangerous rebound hypertension.
options.D: It will cause an immediate permanent loss of taste.

explanation: Spot on! Stopping blood pressure meds abruptly can cause blood pressure to shoot right back up to dangerous levels. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which common side effect is often linked to ACE inhibitors like lisinopril?

options.A: A persistent dry cough
options.B: Extreme darkening of the urine
options.C: Severe yellowing of the eyes
options.D: Uncontrollable muscle twitching

explanation: You nailed it! ACE inhibitors can cause a buildup in the lungs that leads to a nagging, dry cough for some patients. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the main difference between a hypertensive urgency and a hypertensive emergency?

options.A: Emergency involves acute damage to target organs, while urgency does not.
options.B: Urgency occurs only in children, whereas emergency affects adults.
options.C: Emergency can be safely treated at home with herbal teas.
options.D: Urgency involves higher blood pressure numbers than emergency.

explanation: Spot on! An emergency means high blood pressure is actively damaging vital organs like the brain or heart, requiring immediate medical care. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a major long-term complication of uncontrolled high blood pressure?

options.A: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.B: Chronic kidney disease
options.C: Stroke
options.D: Myocardial infarction

explanation: Correct! Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition involving the pancreas, not something directly caused by high blood pressure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is a major goal of community blood pressure screening programs?

options.A: To distribute free surgical equipment to local residents
options.B: To diagnose and treat rare genetic skin disorders
options.C: To replace hospital emergency rooms entirely
options.D: To identify undiagnosed hypertension early before complications occur

explanation: You got it! Since hypertension is 'silent,' community screenings help catch it early so we can prevent strokes and heart attacks. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h7)

question: Why is it often hard to convince patients to take their blood pressure pills every single day?

options.A: Antihypertensive drugs taste extremely sweet.
options.B: Blood pressure medications only work during the rainy season.
options.C: Pills are too large to swallow comfortably.
options.D: Patients often feel fine and may not see the need to take drugs daily.

explanation: Spot on! Because high blood pressure usually doesn't make people feel sick day-to-day, they might mistakenly think they don't need their meds. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h7)

question: What is the main problem in the body that causes diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Defects in insulin production or action
options.B: Overproduction of digestive enzymes
options.C: Excessive secretion of glucagon
options.D: Rapid breakdown of thyroid hormones

explanation: Think of diabetes as a trouble with insulin—either the body isn't making enough of it, or it's not using the insulin it has properly, which leaves too much sugar in the blood. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h1)

question: Over time, why does high blood sugar cause damage to organs?

options.A: Sugar molecules directly injure delicate blood vessels and nerves
options.B: Glucose turns into a toxic acid inside major body organs
options.C: The pancreas stops producing all red blood cells
options.D: Extra sugar blocks the normal flow of oxygen to the lungs

explanation: When blood sugar stays high for too long, it acts almost like sandpaper on the tiny, delicate blood vessels and nerves all over the body. Spotting this early helps us protect our patients! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why do patients with untreated diabetes always feel very thirsty and pee a lot?

options.A: Excess blood sugar pulls large amounts of water into the urine as the kidneys filter it out
options.B: Dehydration is caused by a simultaneous infection in the bladder
options.C: The liver stores extra water to dilute circulating blood sugar
options.D: High insulin levels trick the brain into thinking the body is dehydrated

explanation: When the kidneys try to wash away all that extra sugar, water naturally follows it out. That leads to heavy urination and leaves the patient feeling super thirsty. Makes total sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of insulin at the cellular level?

options.A: It converts dietary protein directly into red blood cells
options.B: It signals the kidneys to absorb more sugar into the bloodstream
options.C: It destroys excess bacteria circulating in the plasma
options.D: It acts as a key to unlock cell receptors and let glucose inside

explanation: You can picture insulin as a tiny key. It unlocks the doors of our body cells so glucose from the food we eat can go inside and give us energy. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the main cause of Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.B: Gradual resistance of body cells to normal insulin
options.C: Temporary hormone changes during pregnancy
options.D: Poor dietary intake of refined carbohydrates

explanation: In Type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system gets confused and mistakenly attacks the insulin-making beta cells in the pancreas. Brilliant to keep this distinction in mind! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h3)

question: How is Type 2 diabetes different from Type 1?

options.A: Type 1 can be cured entirely with proper diet and oral medication
options.B: Type 2 only affects elderly individuals who consume high amounts of sugar
options.C: Type 2 involves insulin resistance and relative deficiency rather than complete beta cell destruction
options.D: Type 1 is caused by lifestyle factors while Type 2 is strictly genetic

explanation: In Type 2, the body still makes insulin, but the cells just don't respond to it well (resistance), and the pancreas can't keep up with the extra demand. You're mastering the basics! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h3)

question: A 45-year-old Nigerian civil servant works a desk job and has central obesity. Which condition is he most at risk for?

options.A: Acute diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Gestational diabetes
options.C: Type 1 autoimmune diabetes
options.D: Type 2 diabetes mellitus

explanation: Sitting for long hours, lack of exercise, and belly fat are classic risk factors for Type 2 diabetes. Seeing how this connects to real life makes clinical rotations much easier! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which lifestyle change is a major reason diabetes is becoming more common in Nigerian cities?

options.A: Engaging in heavy manual farm labor every morning
options.B: Consuming excessive amounts of natural spring water
options.C: Increasing daily intake of green leafy vegetables
options.D: Adopting processed diets and reducing physical activity

explanation: With busy city life, more people eat fast, processed foods and move around less. This shift in lifestyle greatly increases metabolic risks. Great insight for community nursing! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h4)

question: What HbA1c blood test result is generally used to diagnose diabetes?

options.A: 8.0% or higher
options.B: 10.5% or higher
options.D: 6.5% or higher

explanation: An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher shows that blood sugar has been running high over the past three months. It's a key lab value you'll use all the time in practice! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h5)

question: What do the three classic signs of diabetes—polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia—actually mean?

options.A: Frequent headaches, blurred vision, and dizziness
options.B: High blood pressure, rapid heart rate, and fever
options.C: Joint pain, muscle weakness, and skin rashes
options.D: Excessive urination, excessive thirst, and excessive hunger

explanation: Just break down the medical terms: 'uria' relates to urine, 'dipsia' to thirst, and 'phagia' to eating/hunger! Remembering the Greek roots makes nursing terms so much easier. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h5)

question: What is the main lifelong treatment needed for someone with Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Lifelong insulin therapy
options.B: Temporary blood thinners
options.C: Oral metformin tablets only
options.D: Weekly antibiotic injections

explanation: Since the body isn't making insulin at all in Type 1, patients must take insulin every day to survive. You're doing great with your pharmacology basics! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h6)

question: A patient with diabetes looks shaky, dizzy, and is sweating before lunch. What should the nurse do right away?

options.A: Administer the scheduled dose of daily long-acting insulin
options.B: Send a blood sample to the laboratory for an HbA1c test
options.C: Encourage the patient to sleep until the symptoms pass
options.D: Check blood glucose levels and prepare a fast-acting carbohydrate

explanation: Shakiness and sweating are red flags for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Always check the blood glucose first and have a fast sugar source ready! Patient safety comes first. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why are community health screening programs so important for managing diabetes in Nigeria?

options.A: Many individuals have undiagnosed diabetes and only discover it when complications arise
options.B: Community outreach prevents all forms of genetic Type 1 diabetes
options.C: Public testing eliminates the need for personal blood glucose meters
options.D: Screening programs replace the need for prescription medications entirely

explanation: Lots of people walk around with high blood sugar without knowing it. Community screenings help catch it early before severe damage happens. That's true public health nursing! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a main focus of community-level diabetes education?

options.A: Dispelling cultural myths about the causes of chronic illness
options.B: Teaching healthy food substitutions using local ingredients
options.C: Promoting expensive surgical weight-loss procedures for all citizens
options.D: Encouraging affordable physical activity like brisk walking

explanation: Community education focuses on practical, low-cost steps like eating local healthy foods and walking. Expensive surgeries are definitely not standard community advice! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h7)

question: What is the main difference between microvascular and macrovascular complications in diabetes?

options.A: Microvascular conditions involve low blood sugar, while macrovascular conditions involve high blood sugar
options.B: Macrovascular damage is reversible with diet, whereas microvascular damage requires surgery
options.C: Microvascular affects tiny vessels in the eyes, kidneys, and nerves, while macrovascular affects large vessels like the heart and brain
options.D: Microvascular complications only occur in Type 1 while macrovascular only occur in Type 2

explanation: 'Micro' means tiny (eyes, kidneys, nerves), and 'macro' means large (heart, brain). Long-term high sugar hurts both sizes of blood vessels in different ways! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h8)

question: Which acute complication is caused by severe lack of insulin, leading to acid buildup and ketones in Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.B: Peripheral neuropathy
options.C: Severe hypoglycemia
options.D: Diabetic ketoacidosis

explanation: When cells can't get glucose without insulin, the body burns fat instead. This process makes acidic byproducts called ketones, causing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). You're tackling advanced concepts like a pro! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h8)

question: What actually happens when someone has a physical dependence on a drug?

options.A: The complete inability to remember recent events after drinking
options.B: A sudden allergy to chemical substances found in prescription drugs
options.C: The body reacts with unpleasant symptoms when the drug is stopped
options.D: An emotional desire to feel happy without taking any medicine

explanation: Spot on! Physical dependence simply means the body has gotten so used to the drug that it protests with withdrawal signs when the supply cuts off. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why do nurses view substance abuse as a chronic brain condition rather than a lack of willpower?

options.A: It only affects people who have inherited genetic immune deficiencies
options.B: It permanently alters neural pathways and changes how the brain functions
options.C: It prevents the liver from producing enough blood cells for survival
options.D: It is classified as a physical injury caused by accidental trauma

explanation: Exactly! Repeated drug use actually rewires brain chemistry and structure. Seeing it as a medical condition helps us care for patients with real empathy. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which category of substances acts by slowing down brain activity and central nervous system functions?

options.A: Stimulants
options.B: Hallucinogens
options.C: Inhalants
options.D: Depressants

explanation: Correct! Depressants like alcohol put the brakes on the nervous system, which can dangerously lower breathing and heart rates if taken in excess. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h2)

question: A young patient comes in with a racing heart, high blood pressure, and extreme agitation after taking a street drug. Which category is most likely at play?

options.A: Cannabinoids
options.B: Sedatives
options.C: Stimulants
options.D: Depressants

explanation: Spot on! Stimulants rev up the central nervous system, leading to high energy, elevated vitals, and intense jitters or agitation. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h2)

question: What is a major environmental risk factor that can push someone toward substance abuse?

options.A: Living in a house with too many windows
options.B: Having a naturally slow resting heart rate
options.C: Eating a diet low in essential vitamins
options.D: Peer pressure and easy availability of drugs

explanation: That's right! Surroundings matter a lot. Hanging out with peers who use drugs and having easy access makes it much harder to say no. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why do people with untreated mental health challenges sometimes run a higher risk of substance abuse?

options.A: Their bodies process alcohol much faster than healthy people do
options.B: Mental illness completely stops the brain from feeling physical pain
options.C: They may use drugs to self-medicate and escape emotional pain
options.D: Prescription drugs for mental illness always cause chemical addiction

explanation: Spot on. When professional mental health support isn't available, some people unfortunately turn to substances just to numb heavy feelings like anxiety or depression. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which chemical messenger is mainly responsible for the brain's reward system and feelings of pleasure during drug use?

options.A: Hemoglobin
options.B: Dopamine
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Thyroxine

explanation: Nailed it! Dopamine is our feel-good chemical. Drugs flood the brain with it, creating an intense artificial high that tricks the reward system. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h4)

question: Why does someone struggling with long-term drug use need larger doses over time to get the same high?

options.A: The kidneys begin filtering the chemical out of the blood much faster
options.B: The brain reduces its own dopamine production and receptor sites to adapt
options.C: The liver starts storing the drug in fat tissues instead of breaking it down
options.D: The stomach lining thickens and blocks the drug from entering the bloodstream

explanation: Brilliant! This is tolerance in action. The brain tries to protect itself from massive chemical floods by muting its own receptors, meaning you need more of the drug just to feel normal. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which behavioral change is a classic warning sign of potential substance abuse?

options.A: Neglecting work or school responsibilities
options.B: Consistent weight gain and healthy skin tone
options.C: An increased interest in family activities
options.D: Sudden improvement in daily sleep routines

explanation: Correct! When substances take center stage in someone's life, important commitments like classes, work, and family duties usually start slipping away. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why is keeping a close eye on vital signs so crucial when a patient is going through alcohol or sedative withdrawal?

options.A: It helps prove to the patient that they have an active drug problem
options.B: It replaces the need to take blood samples for kidney function tests
options.C: Withdrawal from these substances can cause dangerous and life-threatening physical instability
options.D: Vital signs remain completely normal throughout the entire detox process

explanation: Spot on! Unlike some other substances, alcohol and sedative withdrawal can trigger severe seizures and drastic blood pressure changes. Close monitoring keeps the patient safe. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is the main reason nurses use quick screening tools like the CAGE questionnaire?

options.A: To measure the exact level of vitamins present in the bloodstream
options.B: To quickly identify potential substance abuse or dependence problems
options.C: To calculate the correct dosage of emergency antidote medication
options.D: To diagnose specific mental health disorders like major depression

explanation: Exactly! Screening tools are short, easy-to-use questions that help us spot patients who might need a closer look or professional support for substance use. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h6)

question: A patient is experiencing acute withdrawal tremors and confusion. Which nursing diagnosis should be your top priority?

options.A: Ineffective Health Maintenance
options.B: Chronic Low Self-Esteem
options.C: Deficient Fluid Volume
options.D: Risk for Injury

explanation: Correct! With tremors and confusion, keeping the patient safe from falls, seizures, and self-harm is always the absolute first priority in nursing care. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of medical detoxification in substance abuse care?

options.A: To isolate the patient from all family members during therapy
options.B: To teach the patient new vocational skills for finding employment
options.C: To permanently cure the psychological desire to use drugs again
options.D: To safely clear the substance from the body while managing withdrawal symptoms

explanation: Spot on! Detox is all about physical stabilization—getting the drug out of the system safely while doctors and nurses help manage the rough withdrawal symptoms. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h7)

question: Why is psychological rehab just as vital as physical detox when treating substance dependence?

options.A: It replaces the need for any nursing observation or vital sign monitoring
options.B: It ensures the patient never experiences physical withdrawal symptoms again
options.C: It addresses underlying triggers and teaches healthy coping skills to prevent relapse
options.D: It is the only way to restore normal kidney and liver function after drug use

explanation: Brilliant! Detox cleans out the body, but rehab tackles the emotional and behavioral roots of addiction so the patient can learn new ways to cope without drugs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is the main focus of primary prevention programs for substance abuse in communities?

options.A: Providing emergency medical care for patients suffering from drug overdose
options.B: Educating youth about the dangers of drugs and how to resist peer pressure
options.C: Punishing individuals who sell illegal substances on the street
options.D: Managing acute withdrawal symptoms inside a hospital detox unit

explanation: You got it! Primary prevention stops the problem before it even starts by giving young people the right information and strong coping tools early on. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h8)

question: How do public health policies regarding alcohol and drug sales help protect a community?

options.A: By controlling availability and setting legal boundaries that limit harmful consumption
options.B: By removing the need for nurses to screen patients during health visits
options.C: By completely eliminating the biological need for dopamine in the human brain
options.D: By replacing all illegal drugs with safe prescription alternatives for everyone

explanation: Spot on! Regulations on pricing, sales hours, and public use help keep substances less accessible, which naturally lowers overall rates of misuse in the population. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h8)

question: Which main chemical in tobacco makes it so addictive?

options.A: Ammonia
options.B: Tar
options.C: Carbon monoxide
options.D: Nicotine

explanation: Nicotine is the addictive substance in tobacco that hooks the brain and drives the urge to keep smoking. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why do regular smokers need to smoke more over time to feel the same buzz?

options.A: Their lungs have expanded and require more volume
options.B: Their social circles encourage heavier smoking habits
options.C: Their brains have developed tolerance to the chemical
options.D: The tobacco companies put weaker ingredients in newer packs

explanation: Tolerance happens when the brain gets so used to nicotine that it needs higher amounts to feel that same initial effect. Great job thinking this through! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h1)

question: What is a common tobacco trend among young people in Nigerian cities today?

options.A: A total shift toward chewing raw tobacco leaves exclusively
options.B: A complete halt in all forms of smoking
options.C: The rising popularity of manufactured cigarettes and shisha
options.D: The replacement of tobacco with herbal medicinal teas

explanation: Smart marketing has made manufactured cigarettes and waterpipes (shisha) very popular among urban youth. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h2)

question: How does widespread tobacco use create a double challenge for Nigeria's health system?

options.A: It reduces the overall population so much that clinics have no patients to treat
options.B: It causes nurses to leave public clinics for international job opportunities
options.C: It forces hospitals to buy expensive imported equipment for infectious diseases only
options.D: It requires managing rising lifestyle diseases alongside existing infectious disease challenges

explanation: Clinics have to juggle treating traditional infectious diseases while also handling a growing wave of chronic illnesses caused by tobacco. You are learning fast! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h2)

question: Which tiny, hair-like parts of the respiratory tract get paralyzed and destroyed by cigarette smoke?

options.A: Cilia
options.B: Alveoli
options.C: Bronchioles
options.D: Pleura

explanation: Cilia are the tiny sweeping brushes of the lungs that clear out mucus and dirt. Smoke damages them badly, but understanding this puts you one step ahead! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h3)

question: A 30-year smoker comes in with severe breathlessness and a chronic cough. Which condition affecting the tiny air sacs is most likely the cause?

options.A: Acute bronchitis
options.B: Bacterial pneumonia
options.C: Emphysema
options.D: Pulmonary embolism

explanation: Long-term smoking destroys the delicate walls of the alveoli (air sacs), leading to emphysema and trapped air. You're building solid clinical instincts! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h3)

question: Why do people trying to quit smoking often get sudden cravings when doing routine things, like drinking morning tea?

options.A: Their physical lungs are suddenly damaged by the beverage steam
options.B: The brain has formed strong behavioral links between those routines and smoking
options.C: Their immune system is reacting to dietary changes
options.D: The tea contains hidden traces of chemical nicotine

explanation: Daily habits act as triggers because the brain links those routines directly to smoking. Recognizing this helps us support patients better! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h4)

question: Even after physical withdrawal fades, why is quitting smoking still so tough?

options.A: Commercial cigarettes contain permanent cellular dyes
options.B: Social laws make it illegal to stop smoking abruptly
options.C: The body continues producing natural nicotine forever
options.D: Psychological habits and environmental triggers remain deeply ingrained

explanation: The mental habit and social triggers stick around long after the physical chemicals leave the body. Don't worry if this takes time to master! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h4)

question: In the '5 As' smoking cessation framework, which step means checking if a patient uses tobacco during every clinic visit?

options.A: Assess
options.B: Advise
options.C: Ask
options.D: Arrange

explanation: The 'Ask' step is simply checking and recording whether every patient uses tobacco. Simple, direct, and essential for good nursing care! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h5)

question: During community outreach, a nurse asks a client if they are ready to stop smoking today. Which of the '5 As' is this?

options.A: Analyze
options.B: Advise
options.C: Assist
options.D: Assess

explanation: Checking a patient's willingness and readiness to quit falls right under the 'Assess' step. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which of the '5 Rs' motivational counseling steps helps a patient spot personal barriers and challenges to quitting?

options.A: Rewards
options.B: Roadblocks
options.C: Relevance
options.D: Risks

explanation: Looking at 'Roadblocks' helps patients plan for tough things like stress, urges, and social pressure. You've got a great grasp of patient communication! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h6)

question: A patient says quitting is pointless because their health is already ruined. Which 'R' should the nurse use first to motivate them?

options.A: Relevance
options.B: Rewards
options.C: Repetition
options.D: Readiness

explanation: Connecting quitting directly to their personal health situation makes the conversation meaningful to them. Excellent clinical reasoning! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of using Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) when trying to quit?

options.A: It delivers controlled nicotine doses without toxic tar and carbon monoxide
options.B: It permanently repairs lung tissue damage overnight
options.C: It numbs the throat so the patient can never taste tobacco again
options.D: It immediately cures psychological depression

explanation: NRT gives clean nicotine to ease withdrawal without exposing the body to the dangerous toxins found in cigarette smoke. Brilliant work! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h7)

question: Why do experts recommend combining medication with behavioral counseling instead of using medication alone?

options.A: Counseling addresses the psychological habits while medication treats physical cravings
options.B: Government health insurance policies forbid giving out prescriptions alone
options.C: Medications are too expensive for patients to buy without counseling
options.D: Medications only work if the patient attends weekly support group meetings

explanation: Tackling both the physical craving and the mental habit gives the patient the absolute best chance at success. You're thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h7)

question: Which public health policy is proven to stop young people from starting to smoke?

options.A: Lowering the age restriction for purchasing cigars
options.B: Allowing tobacco companies to sponsor school sports
options.C: Providing free ashtrays in public parks
options.D: Increasing taxation on tobacco products

explanation: Higher taxes raise cigarette prices, making them much harder for price-sensitive teens to afford. Every public health measure counts! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h8)

question: What is the main goal of community nursing advocacy for smoke-free indoor public spaces?

options.A: To protect non-smokers and children from the dangers of secondhand smoke
options.B: To help current smokers reduce their daily cigarette count
options.C: To reduce the government spending on imported medical supplies
options.D: To eliminate all tobacco farming in rural agricultural areas

explanation: Smoke-free rules ensure that people who don't smoke aren't forced to breathe in harmful tobacco smoke. Amazing job completing this session! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h8)

question: How would you simply describe what stress is to a patient?

options.A: A vitamin deficiency caused by poor dietary habits
options.B: A rare psychological disorder requiring lifelong medication
options.C: The body's reaction to demands that disrupt normal balance
options.D: An infectious disease spread through community contact

explanation: Think of stress as your body's natural alarm system kicking in when pressures get too heavy and knock you off balance. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is long-term (chronic) stress tougher on the body than short-term stress?

options.A: It causes immediate physical injury like broken bones
options.B: It lingers over a long period and wears down body defenses
options.C: It only affects people living in rural agricultural areas
options.D: It completely stops the heart within a few seconds

explanation: While a quick burst of stress can help you run from danger, staying stressed for months wears your body down and opens the door to sickness. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h1)

question: When you face sudden stress, which two key hormones do your adrenal glands rush out?

options.A: Adrenaline and cortisol
options.B: Estrogen and progesterone
options.C: Thyroxine and calcitonin
options.D: Insulin and glucagon

explanation: Adrenaline gives you that instant rush of energy (fight or flight), while cortisol helps keep your energy up to handle the stressor. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h2)

question: Why does your digestion temporarily slow down when you are suddenly startled or stressed?

options.A: The stomach stops working permanently due to shock
options.B: Food intake automatically increases during stressful times
options.C: Energy is diverted to muscles and vital organs for defense
options.D: Digestive enzymes turn into stress hormones instantly

explanation: Your body is smart! When danger hits, it pulls energy away from digesting food and sends it straight to your muscles so you can react fast. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is the correct sequence of the three stages in the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)?

options.A: Alarm reaction, exhaustion, resistance
options.B: Alarm reaction, resistance, exhaustion
options.C: Resistance, exhaustion, alarm reaction
options.D: Exhaustion, alarm reaction, resistance

explanation: Easy to remember: First you sound the Alarm, then you Try to resist it, and if it won't stop, your body reaches Exhaustion. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h3)

question: A patient has worried endlessly about money for over a year and now feels constantly exhausted and sick. Which GAS stage is this?

options.A: Alarm stage
options.B: Recovery stage
options.C: Resistance stage
options.D: Exhaustion stage

explanation: When stress drags on too long, the body runs completely out of coping reserves. That's the exhaustion stage where immunity drops. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which of these is a common everyday community stressor in our environment?

options.A: Living in a quiet, peaceful neighborhood
options.B: A balanced diet and regular exercise
options.C: Having too much free time and rest
options.D: Financial instability and high cost of living

explanation: Economic worries and the daily struggle to meet basic needs are massive sources of stress for many people around us. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h4)

question: As a community health nurse, why must you look at environmental factors when assessing a patient's stress?

options.A: Environmental triggers are the only proven cause of mental illness
options.B: External pressures like security and poverty often drive individual stress
options.C: Individual counseling works without knowing the community background
options.D: Nurses are required to fix bad roads and public infrastructure

explanation: An individual's stress rarely happens in a vacuum. Shared hardships like poverty or safety issues play a huge role in how they feel. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h4)

question: How do patients dealing with heavy stress often present themselves in the clinic?

options.A: With sudden weight gain and lower blood pressure
options.B: With visible joy and high energy levels
options.C: With physical complaints like headaches, insomnia, and body pains
options.D: With enhanced memory and sharp focus

explanation: Emotional stress loves to hide in physical symptoms. When patients can't sleep or have endless body aches, stress is often the culprit! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h5)
